title: Who owns AI-generated work (United States)

sources.claim: Thaler v. Perlmutter (D.C. Cir., March 18, 2025) held that the US Copyright Act requires human authorship, upholding the refusal to register an image the applicant said was made entirely by an AI system; the court did not decide how much human contribution is enough for AI-assisted works. The Supreme Court declined review on March 2, 2026.

US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Part 2: Copyrightability (January 29, 2025): given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not give enough human control to make the user the author of the output; human-authored expression, and human selection, arrangement or modification of AI output, can be protected.
Zarya of the Dawn (US Copyright Office, February 2023): the comic's text and the human selection and arrangement of its parts were registrable, but the individual AI-generated images were not.
US Copyright Office registration guidance (March 16, 2023): applicants must disclose AI-generated material that is more than minimal and claim only the human-authored parts.

sections.skill: Apply the US human-authorship requirement and separate settled from open

questions.prompt: What does US copyright require?

choices.text: Any creator at all, including an AI system working completely on its own without a person

questions.intro: In the United States, COPYRIGHT protects works with HUMAN AUTHORSHIP. In Thaler v. Perlmutter (March 18, 2025), a federal appeals court upheld refusing registration for an image the applicant said an AI made entirely by itself; the Supreme Court declined review in March 2026. The US Copyright Office's January 2025 report said prompts alone generally do not make someone the author, while human-written text and human SELECTION, ARRANGEMENT or MODIFICATION of AI output can be protected. SETTLED: purely AI-generated material is not protected. OPEN: exactly how much human contribution is enough.

sections.skill: Compare AI authorship with arranging a flower bouquet

questions.prompt: In the bouquet, what reflects your choices?

choices.text: The individual flowers, which you created yourself from seeds you designed in a lab

questions.intro: If you pick wildflowers and ARRANGE them into a bouquet, the arrangement reflects your choices, but you did not create the individual flowers. Similarly, under the US approach, a person who selects and arranges AI-generated images, and writes the text, may have protectable authorship in those human parts, while the individual AI-generated images themselves are not protected. Where exactly the line falls in harder cases is still being worked out.

sections.skill: Disclose AI material and check current status

questions.prompt: Per the March 2023 guidance, what should a US registration applicant disclose?

choices.text: Nothing, since AI use never needs to be mentioned to the Copyright Office in any application

questions.intro: Two Copyright Office examples help. In Zarya of the Dawn (February 2023), a comic's text and the human selection and arrangement of its parts could be registered, but the individual AI-generated images could not. Its March 2023 guidance asks applicants to disclose AI-generated material that is more than minimal and claim only the human-authored parts. Other countries have their own rules. Courts may still refine where the line falls, so check the current status.
